The Invetero Coquette D10 is one of the static car locations required for Randy's Wish List .

The Coquette can be found in the middle of the restricted area on Waxman Island. It's a yellow supercar next to the water and a red shipping container. You can see it through the gate if you approach from the east.

articles.title: New Avengers: Doomsday Teaser Shows Steve Rogers in Latveria, Potentially Names Doom's Son
articles.summary: Marvel Studios has released yet another Avengers: Doomsday trailer, this one focusing on Steve Rogers doing "what needs to be done" in Latveria.
articles.body:
Marvel Studios has released yet another Avengers: Doomsday trailer, this one focusing on Steve Rogers doing "what needs to be done" in Latveria.

The clip, which is doing the rounds on social media, starts with Rodgers and Peggy Carter’s son asking him if he was a superhero, as we saw and heard in the final trailer released earlier this week.

“There were six of us,” he replies. “We were called the Avengers.”

🚨Novo spot de #AvengersDoomsday com cenas inéditas da Disney Turquia. — Taverna Marvel (@TavernaMarvel) November 27, 2026

🚨Novo spot de #AvengersDoomsday com cenas inéditas da Disney Turquia.

We then get a fun meta joke about Steve Rogers actor Chris Evans having played The Human Torch in the Fox-produced Fantastic Four films — a role he reprised in cameo form in Deadpool & Wolverine.

“So, can you fly?” asks his son, as Thor leaps at Doom for yet another look at that finger block. “Turn into fire,” he continues, as the MCU’s Human Torch, played by Joseph Quinn, hurtles out of a building to spray fire on what looks like a Doom magic-protected device below. “Or shoot lasers out of your eyes?” he adds, referencing Cyclops doing his thing.

“No, I can’t do any of that,” Steve replies with a smirk.

At this point we see new footage of Steve in Latveria, the fictional Eastern European nation ruled by Doctor Doom. He’s standing by some sort of circular device, with Doom’s name on it, and summons Mjölnir. After it flies into his hand, Steve draws lightning power to seemingly strike the device.

As we wonder what this is all about, Peggy answers: “He does what needs to be done.”

We then see Steve flying up towards the camera, hammer first, via the Bifrost. So, in a way, he can fly!

Let’s go back to the circular device Steve was about to hit with the lightning. From the wording on the side, it looks like a tomb of sorts for Victor von Doom’s family. We see ‘Malachi von Doom,’ who we presume is Doom’s deceased son.

If this is a tomb for Doom’s family, why is Steve about to smack it with Mjölnir? Is he trying to break into the grave? Could he be trying to resurrect Doom’s wife and kid? Is that what Peggy meant by "he does what needs to be done"?

Avengers: Doomsday Poster Montage Gallery

The Avengers: Doomsday teasers are coming thick and fast as we head towards launch. Earlier this week we got a first look at Magneto vs Doom (and a failed attempt to rip Doom’s mask off), news of plans for a special tribute to Patrick Stewart , a first look at Kelsey Grammer's Beast , and fears over Bucky’s fate .

Avengers: Doomsday hits theaters December 18.

Wesley is IGN's Managing Editor. Find him on Twitter at @wyp100. You can reach Wesley at wesley_yinpoole@ign.com or confidentially at wyp100@proton.me.

articles.title: 30 First-Person Shooter Masterpieces You Need to Play
articles.summary: From the original corridor shooter pioneers to the incredibly sophisticated genre hybrids of the 2020s, these are the 30 first-person shooter masterpieces you need to play.
articles.body:
Part of the promise of video games is putting yourself in another world, taking control of a character and experiencing adventure and excitement through their eyes. No genre takes this premise quite so literally as the first-person shooter, a pillar of the medium and a fundamental building block of the entire industry. There’s no shortage of shooters out there, but a select few stand above the rest as high-water marks for the art form. These are the 30 first-person shooter masterpieces you need to play

Everything has to begin somewhere. For the first-person shooter, the primordial soup was a group of high school students working at a NASA study program in 1973. They created Maze War, a series of corridors you explored in hunt of another player to shoot. Unbeknownst to those students, they had triggered the start of an evolutionary chain that would lead to the creation of 100-player Warzone lobbies where victorious teenagers teabag the dead.

But the first of something is rarely the best, nor the most influential. And so we look a little further ahead in the timeline to find the real pioneers. Wolfenstein 3D , id Software’s 1992 classic, is undoubtedly one of them. But that Nazi-plagued labyrinth was quickly overshadowed a year later by our first true masterpiece.

If the FPS has a main character, it’s the marine that sits in the middle of Doom ’s HUD. A representation of not just your unseen protagonist but also your health, his chiselled features are progressively marred by blood and bruises as you push on through some of the most focused firefights the genre has ever had to offer. Free from the burden of storytelling and lore, Doom is all about the kill.

And there are so, so many kills. The garish corridors of Mars (and, later, Hell) are perfectly formed containers for exciting, kinetic, and challenging combat encounters. Back in 1993 we couldn’t even look up, but that didn’t stop id Software from assaulting us with an array of demons, both grounded and flying. Survival against such odds is made possible thanks to a small arsenal of weapons so purposeful in their design it makes modern shooters, with their army supply inventory, look like criminal waste – who needs (or even wants) 15 different SMGs when you can have the best shotgun in the business to gun down imps, and the chaingun with an RPM perfectly calibrated to interrupt a cacodemon’s fiery belches?

The early days of first-person shooters were an abstract affair, with blank-slate protagonists gliding through spartan research facilities and gothic labyrinths. The setting was more of a suggestion to keep you moving, bleary brick textures on ray-casted walls for your mute hero to grunt against in search of secret doors. Gamers were more than happy with the arrangement until a potty-mouthed, stogie-chomping, mildly misogynistic meathead showed them a better way.

Apogee’s Duke Nukem 3D brought their EGA sidescrolling hero to a new dimension in the first hit shooter that dared to have a personality. Fully-voiced by Jon St. John, Duke oozed charisma, cracking jokes and one-liners appropriated from ‘80s action cinema. Fittingly, the first level sees Duke dropped onto an LA rooftop and fighting his way into an infested movie theater full of interactive objects, a far cry from the castles and space bases of his contemporaries. This was a first-person shooter that took place in our world, at our time, in places we could actually recognize, albeit with more burning barrels and floating powerups. The first-person POV was designed to help players embody their avatar, and Duke 3D was the first to make the world they inhabited just as immersive.

1999 is arguably the most important year in multiplayer history. Id Software continued to shape the bedrock of the entire FPS genre with Quake 3 Arena, an outstanding multiplayer hit whose engine would go on to power the behemoth that is Call of Duty. But just a few weeks earlier, Epic Games had shipped Unreal Tournament – the studio’s first dedicated PvP game, and the very first cog in the machine that would eventually become Fortnite.

But even 27 years and hundreds of innovators later, Unreal Tournament remains perfectly formed. It is a library of phenomenal level design, with the industrial ramps and slime pools of DM-Deck16 providing the perfect arrangement of height and hazard for the ultimate deathmatch, and the symmetrical halves of the incredibly lean Facing Worlds providing the blueprint for every great Capture the Flag map. The arsenal is fantastic (particularly the ricocheting pellets ejected by the Flak Canon) and the action a gore-soaked adrenaline rush, but it’s the precision-engineered maps that make Unreal Tournament an immortal classic.

Valve does things differently. That’s a truth that goes right back to the developer’s very first game. Doom, Quake, and Unreal all have some kind of story wrapper, but they’re utilitarian – the gunplay is what drives them. Half-Life proved that narrative could be more than just a framework for FPS games. Gordon Freeman’s escape from a laboratory under siege is one of the richest stories a shooter has ever told, and it does it with barely any dialogue. Instead, the very walls and floors of the Black Mesa Research Facility provide the script – each new corridor and chamber the stage for a dramatic alien incursion or eerily quiet reveal. While Half-Life technically does have levels, the lab flows as one whole, continuous space, which cements it as a genuine place rather than a series of maps. The result is an experience that feels incredibly real, which only enhances the horror of your work colleagues being transformed into zombies.

Doom has remained a titan of shooters because it never ages. It’s constantly being reinvented and updated, typically by modding fans who have created some of the original game’s greatest levels. But id Software itself has also approached its hellish masterpiece in brand new ways, and the exceptional 2016 reboot of Doom is gaming’s best example of how to revitalise a franchise.

The hyper-specific focus of the original game remains, but it’s elevated to impossible new heights by the punchiest gunplay you’ve ever pulled the trigger of. Your trusty shotgun rips demons apart, but when that’s not enough you can literally dig your hands in, tearing flesh to not just kill, but to replenish your own life force. This reboot arrived on the tail end of an era where shooters had been obsessed with cover and hunkering down to recover health. Doom said f*ck all that – to mend, you need to maul. And by tearing up the rule book, it restored the franchise’s HP to 100%.

So far, this could easily be mistaken for a list of the best PC games. When it comes to accuracy, the mouse is king, so of course many of the best shooters can be found on PC. But as soon as the analogue stick was invented, a whole new world was unlocked on consoles. While modern logic dictates that you need two sticks to make a shooter work, Nintendo has never been one for conventional thinking. The Nintendo 64 controller had just one analogue stick, and that carried us through one of the most seminal FPS games of all time…

Hailing from an era of Doom clones and developed by a team of novices at Rare, in hindsight it’s incredible that GoldenEye 007 became an iconic trailblazer. Rather than a straight up shooting gallery, its campaign acknowledged James Bond’s secret service employment through encouragement of stealth – there are no health packs here, and gunfire will summon curious guards, so tactical elimination of enemies is often the name of the game. Thankfully, an array of clever gadgets and then-novel tricks, like a sniper rifle with telescopic scope, offered methods of survival beyond just equipping the Klobb SMG for a bit of pray-and-spray.

Of course, the Klobb’s ridiculous fire rate proved incredibly useful in GoldenEye’s unforgettable multiplayer. Featuring a collection of modes with objectives inspired by Bond’s adventures, such as You Only Live Twice’s two-lives-per-player, and The Man With The Golden Gun’s instakill 24-karat blaster, this was (and still is) the splitscreen champion of the world.

Nintendo may be best known as the home of the world’s greatest platformers, but GoldenEye proved you didn’t need a PC to play a groundbreaking FPS. A generation later, the big N continued to innovate: 2002’s Metroid Prime became the GameCube’s most essential shooter by stripping back the shooting.

Yes, you are of course equipped with Samus Aran’s trademark arm cannon, and the surface of Tallon IV is home to plenty of enemies in need of blasting, but Metroid Prime takes a quieter approach to the FPS, prioritizing exploration over explosions. An effective translation of the series’ 2D values into a 3D world, puzzles and platforming are your core verbs here. Unlocking new equipment allows you to enter and survive new regions, and demolishing bosses arms you with an enjoyable selection of tools that ensures the galaxy’s coolest bounty hunter will take down her mark.

Bungie wanted to call its Xbox debut simply “Halo”. It was Microsoft that insisted on the “Combat Evolved” subtitle. As clunky and unnecessary as that addition is, though, it’s impossible to deny that it summarised the entire experience in two words. Back in 2001, Halo was an astonishing leap forward, and its advancements still have the capacity to enthrall a quarter century later. The campaign offers a perfectly balanced blend of tight corridor firefights and freeform, vehicle-friendly sandbox areas. Every single weapon not only feels punchy but fulfills a specific role, from the shield-splitting plasma rifle to the tank-busting SPNKr. Bungie’s star achievement, though, is its enemy AI, which turned the various ranks of the Covenant into a coherent fighting force, working together to flank, flush, and finish you. Responding realistically to incoming grenades and dwindling numbers, the Covenant breathes a genuine sense of life into Combat Evolved’s campaign.

Of course, the multiplayer side of Halo didn’t need artificial intelligence – it had real players. While the explosive mix of Xbox Live and Halo 2 was yet to come, the original game’s splitscreen multiplayer remains a supreme example of how to upgrade classic deathmatch with refined maps, phenomenal weapons, and the wildcard addition of a swerving Warthog.

In the wake of Halo’s arrival, the race was on for PlayStation to find its own “Halo killer”. Several developers attempted, every one of them failed. But that’s not to say the hunt didn’t produce greatness. Guerrilla Games’ Killzone 2 is a master of hard, gritty sci-fi, its WW2-in-space aesthetic elevated to great heights thanks to once-mindblowing graphical quality that remains impressive to this day. All that lends the campaign a distinct atmosphere, but the real joy here is something that spans both single and multiplayer: really, really good guns. There are obvious favourites, like the skull-shattering M4 Revolver and the infantry-chewing StA-3 LMG, but every single one of Killzone 2’s weapons is lovingly crafted, with exceptional reload animations, fantastic audio design, and unique approaches that ensure every single one of them fulfills a distinct battlefield purpose.

It wasn’t enough for Bungie to rewrite the FPS rulebook once. With Destiny , it took many of the ideas that fuelled Halo – unrivalled gunfeel, large environments, deep lore, and intense arena multiplayer – and spliced it with DNA from loot-driven games like Diablo and MMOs like World of Warcraft. The result was initially imperfect, with mission design that felt empty compared to the studio’s previous battlegrounds, as well as an over-reliance on grind. But as Destiny expanded, Bungie refined its online shooter formula, finding unique strength in raids – complex six-player co-op dungeons made up of a mix of fierce combat, cryptic puzzles, and tough boss encounters. By the time of Rise of Iron’s Wrath of the Machine and its spectacular Siege Engine, it was more than clear that Bungie had struck gold a second time.

Anyone who loves FPS games will reject the term “mindless shooter”, but there are plenty of gun games that certainly rely on reflexes more than mental aptitude. Serious Sam isn’t remotely concerned with your forward thinking or tactical planning. But, around the turn of the millenium, the genre saw a notable shift away from pure run-and-gun into more cerebral designs. These games thought outside the box – just what could a shooter played from first-person be?

For developer Ion Storm, the answer was a cyberpunk conspiracy thriller where progression through the story had no rules. Deus Ex begins with a choice: will you arm yourself with a tranquiliser crossbow, a sniper rifle, or a rocket launcher?

They’re more than just weapons – each option makes it clear that there are a multitude of ways to tackle the oncoming storm. Will you stealthily maneuver around the terrorists who have set up camp in New York City? Headshot them from afar? Or blow your enemies to smithereens? This guiding light asks you to consider the wider possibilities – if a door is locked, could you sneak in another way? Or can you simply blow it off its hinges? The answer to both is yes. And those solutions are arguably two of the most basic approaches on offer. Deus Ex is smart, and even 25 years later it’s easy to stumble across new possibilities on repeat playthroughs.

The series had a brief modern resurgence with two brilliant prequel games – Human Revolution and Mankind Divided – although both are arguably less complex than their parent. But even if few have rivalled its malleability, Deus Ex opened the FPS up and gave it permission to think much, much bigger.

The System Shock games of the late ‘90s whisked us away to abandoned space stations, where the story of their demise was gradually revealed through audio logs recorded by the long-dead. The series' successor, BioShock , adopted that framework while doubling down on the action. It loaded you up with not just an arsenal of guns, but also a collection of mutant abilities – including ice blasts that could freeze and fireballs that could melt – that proved the shock to the system that the FPS desperately needed in the late 2000s.

Developer Irrational Games' most striking achievement, though, was creating a post-fall world that felt truly tragic. The underwater city of Rapture will forever be one of gaming’s best locations – its sprawling corridors and chambers hauntingly drawn in art deco brass and wood, populated by insane survivors, and given life by the fascinating ecosystem of gene-harvesting Little Sisters and their Big Daddy protectors. Combined with a story that smartly challenges not just Ayn Rand’s controversial politics, but also the assumptions of the player at the controls, BioShock is one of gaming’s unforgettable triumphs.

Irrational wasn’t just making philosophical statements in the 2000s, though – it also created one of history’s greatest tactical shooters. SWAT 4 puts you in command of a team of armed officers and deploys you into a series of crime scenes across New York City, where you’ll need to deal with objectives torn from the headlines. Bomb threats, hostage situations, nightclub shootings, and even hauling in a deranged serial killer are just some of the situations you’ll need to assess and contain.

SWAT is dedicated to realism, so not only do you have to carefully order your team to scout rooms and issue orders in the correct sequence, but you also have to follow strict rules of engagement. Deaths are to be avoided at all cost, so non-lethal weapons are often your best option, and all suspects need to be arrested to achieve the optimum outcome. It all makes for an incredibly methodical shooter that rewards patience, planning, and perfect aim.

There’s not much you can really do to innovate on the FPS formula. Different kinds of guns, unique levels, or interesting mechanics only go so far to dress up the core “pull trigger to make thing die” mode of interaction, and first-person brain-burners like Portal, while ingenious, don’t quite live up to the “shooter” side of the equation. Superhot is the exception, turning the core FPS verbs of movement and shooting into an intricate, mesmerizing puzzle.

The 2016 indie sensation introduces a simple twist: time only moves when you do. Charging red enemies, rendered as stylized polygon humanoids, slow to a crawl while their bullets freeze in mid-air, letting you look around and plan your precious actions. You can shoot a pistol out of their hand, empty the magazine into your foe, fling the empty weapon at another and grab their shotgun before they can pull the trigger. SUPERHOT is a triumph of trial-and-error design made palatable by quick restarts and a huge possibility space. We haven’t seen anything like it since, save for SUPERHOT VR, which turns the clever experiment into a trippy, full-body experience that’s arguably the superior way to play.

Valve’s dedication to authentic reality has guided Half-Life through a couple of industry-leading breakthroughs. Half-Life 2’s revolutionary physics introduced the laws of gravity in a way that has never truly been matched. But Valve’s most impressive reality has been virtual – Half-Life: Alyx is so ridiculously good that it alone (almost) justifies the cost of a VR headset. Transporting you onto the streets of City 17, this is a classic narrative FPS campaign completely recalibrated for virtual reality.

Your own limbs’ physical reflexes can’t compare to the twitch controls of a mouse and keyboard, so Half-Life’s famously slippery firefights have been replaced with smaller scale battles. That may initially sound like a backstep, but the tension of being in a lethal shootout has never felt so real. Meanwhile, the zombie scares are dialed up to 11 (one of the best sequences asks you to literally cover your own mouth to mask your panicked breathing, lest an undead beast find you), and puzzles have been formatted to make full use of 3D space and tactile props. It all adds up to a world that you can really feel, and an adventure that’s more immediate than anything on a flat screen. It’s the best shooter the format has offered, but unfortunately few studios have the resources to follow in Valve’s footsteps.

FPS games began as cramped affairs, trapped in mazes scrounging for keycards or pitted against opponents in bespoke arenas. The format is well-suited for ripping and tearing through demons or teabagging noobs in Midship, but one of the biggest benefits to a first-person perspective is immersion, the idea that we’re looking into an imaginary world through someone else’s eyes. It’s a format that invites exploration, and some of the genre’s greatest games make the most of a wide-open world.

The first two Metro games are deeply atmospheric linear shooters that inject the rough shape of Half-Life with an overdose of grim Eastern European horror. They’re good, but the series’ third entry, Metro Exodus , is a genuine all-timer. Released from Moscow’s underground tunnels and sent to find your destiny on the apocalyptic surface, you’re free to approach a chain of open hub worlds in any way you wish, be that striking from the shadows or unloading both barrels into anything that moves. A mix of smart human enemies and vicious mutants ensures all combat encounters keep you on your toes, and you’ll need to master a multitude of playstyles in order to effectively survive.

If those expertly designed open environments were all Exodus had going for it, then it’d still be a fantastic FPS. But it’s elevated to masterpiece status by its story, which neatly interlocks with the game’s brutal combat mechanics to create one of the most effective horror experiences of the era.

The FPS doesn’t get much bigger than Cyberpunk 2077 . CD Projekt Red’s sci-fi masterpiece follows many of Deus Ex’s cues, including a vast array of body augmentations to unlock fascinating new playstyles, and level design that allows stealthy infiltrations, tactical hacking, and all-out gunfights. But unlike its leather-clad Y2K cousin, Cyberpunk 2077 is an epic-scale RPG set in a sprawling open world city.

The narrative demands of that massive footprint means 2077 is second to none when it comes to worldbuilding – every street corner, market arcade, and towering megablock bleeds lore and environmental storytelling. As the rough-and-ready mercenary, V, you’ll take on seedy jobs featuring some of the genre’s most compelling storylines, from edge-of-your-seat espionage infiltrations to meditations on sin. In short, it has all the top-shelf quest design you’d expect from the developers of The Witcher, but you can make your enemies explode with guns that shoot homing bullets. It’s nothing short of preem.

Ubisoft is one of the main culprits behind the modern open-world formula. Through Assassin’s Creed, the French developer popularized many of the genre’s most recognizable tropes, from climbing towers to reveal the landscape, enemy outposts scattered throughout progress-gated zones, and a minimap clogged with hundreds of icons. Far Cry 3 isn’t Ubisoft’s first attempt at an open world, but it’s the first time that the series took the lessons learned from its third-person contemporaries and applied them through a first-person lens.

Coming off of the unfriendly, unforgiving, and still-unmatched intensity of Far Cry 2, the third game is where the series entered the triple-A canon. It applies the Assassin’s Creed framework to an uncharted island, with gorgeous tropical visuals placed front and center in your field of view. The gunplay and exploration are top-notch, but what distinguishes Far Cry 3 is its story and characters. Michael Mando’s star-making performance as the unhinged and volatile Vaas steals the show, while your own avatar Jason Brody grows from a clueless party bro captured by pirates into an apex predator with a magic skill tree tattoo, a wish-fulfilling power fantasy that only a first-person perspective can truly provide.

You can’t have an FPS without guns. Lots of guns. Borderlands took this notion to the extreme, with a procedurally generated plethora of pew-pews that numbered in the tens of millions. Guns that dish out elemental damage, guns that explode when you throw them, guns with reverse recoil that get more accurate as you fire. It’s an entire language of guns, a lingua franca of firearms, and by the end you’ll be intimately familiar with the pros, cons, and quirks of the eight manufacturers who made them.

Borderlands brought Diablo-style drops to first-person shooters and paved the way for future looter-shooters like The Division and Destiny, and it made such a splash in large part due to the overwhelming personality of its world. While the vibrant cel-shading and intense encounters still hold up, the character writing can seem cringe through our modern sensibilities, though that’s largely because of how influential the series became. Borderlands 2 , starring the unforgettable antagonist Handsome Jack, is the high point and easily stands on its own.

Does New Vegas even count as a first-person shooter? It is first and foremost an RPG, after all, from one of the all-time great studios at the top of their game. The initial promise when Bethesda bought the franchise was “Oblivion with guns,” but Fallout 3 was less than stellar when it came to shooting. Obsidian improved on the foundation, introducing ironsights to make players less reliant on the methodical, turn-based-ish VATS system. Gunplay is further fleshed out by a bigger arsenal, weapon mods, and craftable specialty ammo, though the action on its own can’t really hang with most entries on this list.

Where Fallout: New Vegas excels is, of course, in story and character. The betrayed Courier left for dead in the desert creates a customized journey in every playthrough, navigating the complex factions that call the Mojave Wasteland home and living with the consequences of their choices. Endearing companions and fascinating antagonists give our quests meaning, while the aesthetic and lore of Fallout have never shone brighter than under the sun-bleached Nevada sky. Lots of other shooters have embraced RPG storytelling, but there’s never been another New Vegas.

First-person shooters have never been a solo affair. The most primordial iterations on massive mainframes pit players against each other, and as the genre grew so did the thirst for competition. Simple games of hide and seek became thrilling tests of skill and reflex while LAN parties paved the way for Xbox Live and our modern online infrastructure. Multiplayer is the FPS in its purest form, and if you disagree, we’d be happy to 1v1 you over it.

The notion of Blizzard, the developers behind top-down, zoomed-out strategy games and online RPGs, crafting a competitive, high-octane first-person shooter seemed dubious at first. Overwatch , however, triumphed by doing what Blizzard does best: borrowing from everyone else. The same way they lifted hulking green orcs and armored blue space marines from Warhammer, Blizzard took the class system and objective-first design from Team Fortress 2, fused it with the cooldown management and counterpicking of MOBAs, and slathered the whole package in a glossy layer of Pixar charm.

In a genre like FPS that tends to skew more hardcore, Overwatch was truly for everyone. You could casually enjoy the charming characters in Quick Play, scrape against your Platinum plateau in Ranked, or chase the esports dream in a huge pro scene that arose almost overnight. Like any live service game, Overwatch has changed drastically over the course of its existence, and most veterans can point out the moment where they felt it left them behind: nerfing Mercy’s ult, Brigitte and the infamous GOATS meta, role lock, the cancelled PvE experience and the strange saga of Overwatch 2. These evolutionary shifts are common and even necessary for a long-running multiplayer title to survive, and the game is still going strong today as a result, but that first year or so was pure magic, cementing Overwatch as a modern masterpiece.

Who cares about Quake campaigns? Not John Carmack, the id Software co-founder who famously likened video game plots to those of pornography in terms of importance. Like its contemporary Unreal Tournament, 1999’s Quake 3 Arena eschews any real single-player content in exchange for bot-based skirmishes that simulate the game’s true draw: a high-octane contest of skill and strategy that demands total command of aim, movement, and map knowledge.

Quake 3 is spartan by modern standards. There’s no aiming down the sights here– you won’t have time, since the second you stop moving at ludicrous speed you’ll be fragged out of existence by a railgun blast. You won’t find upgrade systems and character progression to boost your K/D here. In Quake 3 the only improvement is self-improvement. The only way to win is to learn the maps, control the items, and above all else, hit your shots. Quake 3 Arena and the community that coalesced around it helped carry competitive gaming into the new millennium with a bevy of fan-made mods and modes that built on the base game’s purity of pwnage.

Many of the multiplayer shooters on this list are surprisingly small in scale, where you battle alone or with a handful of teammates across a fairly limited map. EA and DICE’s Battlefield series blows all that up in spectacular fashion, with vast conflicts involving dozens of combatants spanning destructible environments that require an entire fleet of vehicles to navigate. It’s all out war in FPS form, and you’re in the driver’s seat.

The series has seen its share of swings and misses through the decades, but in aggregate the highs outweigh the lows. From the original Battlefield 1942, to the HD reinvention of Battlefield 3, and the bold left turn of Battlefield 1, DICE has usually met the industry moment and offered a viable, sometimes superior alternative to Call of Duty’s dominance. When it comes to masterpieces, one game in the series stands out as a complete package: Battlefield: Bad Company 2 . The game’s punky, irreverent attitude, loveable squad of ragtag misfits, and a solid single-player campaign are the icing on top of a masterfully crafted and balanced multiplayer experience. You’d do well with nearly any Battlefield, but Bad Company 2 brings the most joy.

In the military, there’s a concept called “the suck,” a catch-all term for the mind-numbing mundanity, back-breaking labor, danger and suffering that defines the days of those who serve. Arma is a video game series that embraces the suck, that attempts to capture the miserable conditions of combat from the comfort of your computer.

Games like CoD and Battlefield do everything they can to avoid the suck. They’re all about empowerment, getting you in the action as fast as possible with the tools and abilities you need to cap objectives and rack up kills. Arma asks a lot more of you. You fine-tune every decision of the tactical simulation as you fight and die across an island spanning hundreds of square kilometers. You reckon with exhaustion and fatigue and the weight of your loadout while eyeballing bullet drops in the accurately modeled ballistics amid an unforgiving damage model that will end you in an instant.

Arma’s legacy goes beyond just “really hard shooters,” however. DayZ began as an Arma 2 mod that inspired a vast army of open-world survival sims. The DayZ mod, in turn, was transformed into PlayerUnknown’s Battlegrounds, sparking the Battle Royale revolution that begat Fortnite, Warzone, Apex Legends, and countless others. For a game that’s so unfriendly to play, its generosity to modders allowed Arma to birth something far bigger.

Can’t we all just get along? The multiplayer conversation around FPS is predominantly centered on competition, but there’s plenty of fun to be had in fighting with, not against, your friends to fend off an escalating horde of enemies. Co-operative shooters can offer some of the most intense experiences in all of gaming, and they don’t get much better than Left 4 Dead 2 .

Valve didn’t waste any time cranking out a sequel to its 2008 hit Left 4 Dead, which thrust players into the role of four survivors bursting with personality as they struggled through a zombie apocalypse in campaigns presented like a grindhouse cinema matinee. Valve drew sharp criticism for moving on from the slightly flawed original after only a year, as Left 4 Dead 2 made the first game more or less obsolete.

What’s fascinating about Left 4 Dead 2 is that there’s really nothing like it anymore. No one has pushed the AI “Director,” which analyzed how players were doing and adjusted the experience mid-game for maximum tension, much further. The asymmetry of L4D2’s versus mode, where opposing players control superpowered special infected, found its heirs in modern horror games like Dead by Daylight and Halloween, which pit only one beefed-up monster against a squad of victims. Horde modes have similarly fallen out of favor for bigger co-op sandboxes, with the closest cousin probably being Helldivers 2. Coming at the start of the pop-culture zombie boom and the height of Valve’s beast-mode Orange Box era, we may never see a co-op shooter with this much sauce again.

Twenty-five masterpieces isn’t too shabby for a genre that can be reduced to “click things to make them die,” and we still aren’t finished. The following five first-person shooters represent the absolute best the format has to offer, the true titans of their field. Speaking of which…

Many a masterpiece is built from the bones of something that showed a lot of promise but didn’t quite work– Picasso famously painted several of his Blue Period classics on top of earlier portraits and landscapes he’d abandoned. Titanfall, from CoD masterminds Jason West and the late Vince Zampella, was similarly half-formed when the series debuted. It delivered on the dev’s trademark twitch action with a wall-running, sci-fi twist, while the MOBA-style action involved farming NPC grunts to summon your Titan, a hulking yet surprisingly nimble machine that let you dominate the battlefield. It was an intriguing gimmick that controlled beautifully, switching from boots-on-the-ground infantry combat to towering mech battles in an instant, but the game felt incomplete without a meaningful single-player component.

Respawn addressed the lack of campaign in the first Titanfall by creating one of the all-time greats in Titanfall 2 . You are Jack Cooper, rifleman in the Frontier Militia, who finds himself piloting a Titan bequeathed to him by his dying mentor. Over the course of the breezy, perfectly-paced story, Cooper and BT-7274 form an irreplaceable buddy cop bond. Through bloodshed and banter we and Cooper come to love the big lunk, caring deeply for this literally faceless machine.

The campaign is split across nine missions built around “action blocks,” scenarios that each showcase a single idea. Into the Abyss sends you on a desperate search for your best pal BT through an assembly-line gauntlet in an underground factory, while the Ark is an aerial chase through the skies of Typhon. The most celebrated mission, Effect and Cause, introduces time travel into the mix, allowing you to swap between a ruined building and its pristine past in an extremely clever triumph of design that could easily carry its own game.

Titanfall 2 failed to meet sales expectations, but again, not every masterpiece is defined by financial success. Just ask Van Gogh. What makes a masterpiece is the way they move us, how we remember them through the years, and the countless other artists they inspire.

Doom is the blueprint for the modern FPS, so there are a lot of expectations for a Doom game that dares to reinvent it. Doom 2016 was more of an upgrade, bringing the old feel up to speed for a new generation. Doom Eternal pushes beyond the bounds of boomer shooters into something completely different.

In Doom 2016, the super shotgun can carry the Slayer through most encounters without breaking a sweat, but the economy of Eternal demands more variety. Resources are scarce, making glory kills a must, finishing off your foes in particular ways to replenish yourself. Ammo is harder to come by, and so is the chainsaw fuel that makes it magically erupt from demonic viscera. Sturdier demons require specific weapons and tactics to take down. All of it forces you to rely on more of your arsenal to survive every hellish encounter, working nearly every button on the controller with attacks, belches, and things that go boom.

FPS is traditionally the realm of Western developers, a genre born in Texas and still dominated by American and European studios. Doom Eternal is the first to feel like a Japanese character action game, Devil May Cry from behind Doomguy’s visor, double dashing through demon-infested skies raining bullets on the swarms above and below. It rewards skill and acrobatics and demands mastery of your inputs if you dream of surviving the Super Gore Nest. It’s a marvel that you’re not awarded S-ranks for stylish slaying. Some prefer the stripped-down simplicity of Doom 2016, particularly its lighter touch on lore, but Doom Eternal is unlike any other FPS on the market, a gamer’s game that must be experienced to truly comprehend its carnage.

Everyone plays Call of Duty. Your cousin plays Call of Duty. The guys on Love Island play Call of Duty. If the algorithm brought you here, statistically speaking you probably play Call of Duty. First-person shooters are the main and often only way some people interact with video games at all, and it’s all thanks to Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare .

The franchise was still in a healthy spot in 2007, though the World War 2 setting was becoming rote after years of industry exploitation. Gamers were ready to move on from the six-year period that defined the 20th century for something that reflected the less morally sound conflicts of the world outside their window. Modern Warfare was exactly what FPS needed.

Infinity Ward delivered a globetrotting, blockbuster war story with Tom Clancy verisimilitude and a summer movie scale. Combat is big and bombastic, with regenerating health and endless swarms of enemy soldiers for us to ADS out of existence. More importantly, CoD 4’s multiplayer unleashed an addictive rush of unlockables, customization, and killstreaks. It was an experience that would one day become worth drinking Mountain Dew for, if only for the double XP, but the original Modern Warfare best represents the balance of design and dopamine that cemented the first-person shooter as the public face of gaming.

Counter-Strike is a video game in the same sense that chess is a board game: technically true, but it has ascended so far beyond the category it belongs to that it exists in a space all its own. And just like the rules of chess have been static for centuries, changing anything fundamental about CS is tantamount to sacrilege, like adding free throws to baseball. We’re specifically including Counter-Strike 2 because that’s just how those fundamentals are currently packaged, but it’s not all that different from the mod that came out last millennium. Counter-Strike simply is , and no one can touch it.

Two teams of five players must either plant a bomb or defuse it. Each round opens with a buying phase, where your performance dictates what you can afford to bring into battle. Winning requires knowing where to place your crosshair to catch an opponent as they turn a corner, which angles to hold, and even which rounds to sacrifice on purpose. It’s the kind of game you practice for, with aim trainers and minutely dialed-in DPI settings on your mouse. Counter-Strike isn’t something you really approach casually, yet it’s the most-played game on all of Steam, regularly peaking at well over a million players on any given day.

Counter-Strike has no campaign to speak of, but there’s an incredible story behind the game itself. It began as a free mod for Half-Life in 1999, before Valve quickly snapped up the property and hired its creators. CS is the ultimate realization of the PC FPS scene’s DIY spirit, a game made by gamers as a gift to other gamers, and everything is downstream from there. The legendary de_dust map was made by a bedroom coder, as were Gun Game and the mod that would become Prop Hunt, both hugely influential in the wider FPS space. No matter how slick the tournaments get or how big the prize pools grow, there remains a refreshing lack of corporate gloss to Counter-Strike. It’s the FPS that belongs to everyone.

Half-Life 2 ’s unforgettable onboarding experience begins in City 17, with Gordon Freeman picking up a can under the grating gaze of Dr. Breen. Every new chapter unlocks a new facet of the gameplay experience, from blasting through canals on an airboat to find the gravity gun at Black Mesa East and putting it to the test in the boobytrapped town of Ravenholm. Half-Life 2’s Havok physics sent shockwaves through the industry, basically mandating the presence of seesaw puzzles and collapsible scaffolds for years to come.

Half-Life 2 achieves something special in its embodiment of Gordon Freeman. It’s rare to vanish so completely into an avatar, but we find ourselves subsumed by the geeky MIT grad who once had a ponytail. The game’s stakes and drama don't come through cutscenes, they’re around us all the time as expertly staged scenes large and small. It’s the purest form of first-person storytelling that’s rarely been equaled.

Half-Life 2 is unbelievable. It’s impossible for a character created from 8,000 polygons to make us feel something without facial-captured pathos from scanned-in A-list actors. It’s inconceivable that a game forced to launch through a loathed new DRM scheme could turn it into the industry’s most dominant platform. It’s unthinkable that a game made before the age of ironsights and regenerating health could stand as a timeless pinnacle for what an FPS can achieve. If you could only play one first-person shooter in your lifetime, Half-Life 2 would show you exactly what they stand for.

Thanks for reading, everyone. Did any of your favorites not make the list? What do you think makes an FPS masterpiece? Should we have included Portal? Leave a comment, let us know, and stay tuned to IGN for more first-person fragging fun.

articles.title: Denis Villeneuve Was 'Deeply Disappointed' by Disney's Decision to Release Avengers: Doomsday on the Same Day as Dune: Part Three
articles.summary: Denis Villeneuve has revealed his disappointment at Disney's decision to release Avengers: Doomsday in theaters on the same day as Dune: Part Three.
articles.body:
Denis Villeneuve has revealed his disappointment at Disney's decision to release Avengers: Doomsday in theaters on the same day as Dune: Part Three .

Doomsday was initially due out on May 1 this year, but was delayed to December 18 — a date Dune 3 had already claimed. Because of the clash, Avengers: Doomsday misses out on an Imax release, with Villeneuve’s trilogy-ender having already snapped up exclusivity for the big screens.

In a new interview with Time , Villeneuve ran through the various release challenges the Dune movies have endured, and said he thought that with Part Three, he’d finally have a clear run of it.

“Listen, I will be honest,” he began. “The first Dune came out at the end of the pandemic. We made a great box office in a very rough environment. But we had the winds against us. Then the second movie, same thing. We were meant to release in the fall, and we had to release at the end of winter because of the two Hollywood strikes. We had success, but it was not easy. The third time, I said to myself, ‘Finally, there is no pandemic, no strike in sight. We will have a normal release.’ Then Disney put the biggest franchise of all time against us. I’m no fool. Those movies are a mammoth.

“So I was deeply disappointed. But we had committed to this date, to Imax. It was impossible to move. So I accepted my fate, praying to the gods of cinema. Dune is not a mammoth like the Avengers, but it’s a sexy little animal that has a lot of firepower, and I hope we will survive. It could be one of the biggest box-office weekends of all time because of both movies. Am I in competition with the Avengers? Absolutely not. It’s a T. rex. But I stand proud because I think the film delivers.”

Avengers: Doomsday is expected to be one of the biggest movies of all time, with a box office haul Disney will hope matches up to previous Avengers films. It’s thought December 18 could be the largest box office weekend ever, when you factor in Dune 3’s launch. Fans have dubbed the dual release ‘DunesDay,’ in a sort of sci-fi heavy follow-up to 'Barbenheimer.'

Avengers: Doomsday Poster Montage Gallery

But will Dune 3 benefit from Avengers: Doomsday’s release or suffer from it? Villeneuve is putting a brave face on the situation here — I wouldn’t be surprised if there’s plenty of worry internally.

According to the New York Times , Legendary Entertainment and Warner Bros. spent an estimated $200 million to make Dune 3, excluding marketing. The publication suggests the two movies could cannibalize each other, with Disney pushing its new Infinity Vision label for existing large-format screens in a bid to compete with Dune’s Imax exclusivity. If Disney’s marketing works, Avengers could draw dollars away from lucrative Dune Imax ticket sales.

Whatever happens with Dune 3, Villeneuve is moving on to Bond next. “I don’t sleep a lot right now because it’s like I have electricity in my veins thinking about this new project,” he told Time. “It is so different. I spent 10 years of my life in the sun talking about a specific color palette, thinking about ways to embrace natural light. I adore being on Arrakis, but I think it’s healthy to step away.”

articles.title: Save 40% Off the Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 Sport Headphones Gift Edition in Amazon Exclusive Rose Gold for Black Friday
articles.summary: Features bone conduction technology that makes it the best headphones for street runners.
articles.body:
If you enjoy listening to music while you run or work out, then you should consider getting a headset that's specifically designed for it. Shokz is one of the best known and well-respected sport headphone brands and, fortunately for you, the Shokz Black Friday Sale has officially kicked off on Amazon .

As part of this sale, Amazon has dropped the price of the Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 open-ear wireless sport headphones in rose gold from $180 to just $119.99 with free shipping. The rose gold color is exclusive to Amazon. This particular set comes in premium gift packaging, in case you want to surprise a lucky someone this holiday season.

40% Off the Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 Sport Headphones

Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 Open-Ear Wireless Bone Conduction Sport Headphones

The OpenRun Pro 2 looks like a neckband style headphone except that a lightweight titanium band connecting the two ear pieces wraps around the back of your head instead of resting on your neck. This design does an excellent job of keeping everything in place, perfect for active exercise.

Instead of the traditional method of sending sound vibrations to your eardrums, the OpenRun Pro uses bone conduction technology to send vibrations through your cheekbones directly to your inner ear. As such, the headphones are actually placed in front of your ear instead of on your ear. The biggest advantage is that you can fully hear your surroundings; if you like running on streets, for example, you'll be aware of everything that's going on around you while your music is playing.

OpenRun Pro 2 is an obvious upgrade over the Open Run Pro

The OpenRun Pro 2 is a substantial update over its predecessor. The most noticeable upgrade is arguably the switch from a proprietary magnetic charging cable to the USB Type-C standard. Another significant upgrade is the sound quality.

While the original OpenRun Pro has good bass response, it is slightly hampered by the fact that it produces tiny vibrations that are noticeable and sometimes ticklish or distracting. The new OpenRun Pro 2 utilizes Shok's DualPitch technology to virtually eliminate vibrations. Other smaller changes include increased battery life and improved mic quality.

The Shokz OpenRun are the best earbuds for exercise

I have a pair of AirPods Pro that I use regularly, but I always set them aside for the OpenRun Pros when I run. The Transparency mode on the AirPods Pro does work well for most situations, but they still can't compare to the awareness you get without having any buds plugging up your ears. In my experience these headphones stay in place extremely well and the sound quality is great compared to other sport headphones I've tried.

Squishies! Kids love them and can’t get enough. Packs of kids roam the streets at all hours of the night, seeking their next squishy fix. Meanwhile, everything with a Needoh logo on it is sold out everywhere, or only available for jacked-up prices from scalpers.

Here’s a potential solution: Right now Woot is running a Black Friday toy sale that includes lots of squishies on sle for over 50% off. They’re not Needoh brand, but they squish and they’re on sale. And if your kids are young enough, they won’t know the difference anyway. Better yet, if you enter promo code BIGFRIDAY, you’ll get an extra 20% off the already-discounted rate. And if you’ve never made a purchase from Woot, you’ll get 30% off. The sale ends December 7, but the promo code only lasts until November 29.

Squishy Dumpling + Butter Squishy Combo Pack

Woot, for those who don’t follow such things, is a subsidiary of Amazon, so it’s legit. You can even use your Amazon login credentials to complete the purchase using your saved method of payment. Woot often has items on clearance for deeply discounted prices. But stock doesn’t tend to last very long, so grab what you want sooner rather than later.

So what kinds of squishies are we talking about? Squishy butter sticks are available on sale. A butter and dumpling combo pack is 53% off, before the extra promo code deal. You can get squishy holiday dumplings, squishy holiday cubes, squishy cheese, bananas, and watermelon. There’s plenty available, and it’s not going to squish itself. These make excellent stocking stuffers if nothing else.

Sure, some of them have tacky surfaces that will collect dust and lint. Some will inevitably be popped by wretched children and make a mess on the carpet or couch. That’s just life. And no, they’re not Needoh brand, but unless you get lucky at a brick-and-mortar store, you’re probably not going to find any Needoh squishies at MSRP anywhere before Christmas. These are discounted squishies that you can actually buy right now – and that's good enough for me.

articles.title: Resident Evil Requiem, Silent Hill: Townfall and More Horror Games See Big Discounts for Black Friday
articles.summary: Black Friday sales have featured some great discounts on horror games so far, including both Resident Evil Requiem and Silent Hill: Townfall on PS5 hitting $30.
articles.body:
As a big fan of horror games, I've been so happy to see how stacked this year's Black Friday sale is with spooky releases. That includes Resident Evil Requiem and Silent Hill: Townfall on PS5 down to $30 a piece, Silent Hill 2 on sale for $20, and (my favorite finds so far) Resident Evil 2 , Resident Evil 3 , and Resident Evil 7 down to just $13.

If that sells out, the good news is it's available across all platforms for just $40 at Amazon. Silent Hill: Townfall is also worth a spin. I had an amazing time playing immersing myself in the eerie town of St. Amelia and unraveling main character Simon Ordell's story along the way.

Some of the best Black Friday horror game deals have been on older Resident Evil releases. RE2, RE3, and RE7 have dropped to just $13 at Amazon, while RE4 is available for $14. Even Resident Evil Village is on sale right now for just $18. All five come out to $70.55 together, or about the cost of Resident Evil Requiem at its usual full price. That's a lot of Resident Evil for not a lot of money.

While horror games have been some of my favorite finds for Black Friday so far, they're not the only game deals available. Make sure to check out our roundups of the best PS5 , Xbox , and Nintendo deals to see what else is on sale right now.

articles.title: Magic: The Gathering Play Booster Boxes Are up to 50% Off at Amazon for Black Friday
articles.summary: Three Booster Boxes are on sale, and you can save big on the Starter Collection, too - ideal for new and intermediate players.
articles.body:
Magic’s busy year might have you wondering how in the multiverse, you can keep up with it all, but thankfully, Amazon has some handy Black Friday deals to help fill in the gaps in your collection.

Across its catalog, there are savings to be found on Booster Boxes from this year, as well as a product I’d highly recommend: The Starter Collection from Foundations. Here’s what’s on offer, and how much you can save.

Sadly, the following are all Play Booster boxes. That means they’re ideal for building a collection without spending a ton of money, but they do have fewer chances at rare cards than the much pricier Collector Boosters. Plus, those are also harder to find.

The Best Amazon Magic: The Gathering Deals This Black Friday

Kicking us off is the oldest set of the Play Booster Boxes on offer, albeit not by much. Marvel’s Super Heroes was a huge step up from the Spider-Man set, and while your interest will naturally vary depending on how much you want the likes of Iron Man and Captain America cards in your Magic: The Gathering collection, we can’t argue with a good deal.

And, that’s exactly what Amazon is offering, with a $104.90 Play Booster Box down from $147.95 - at least according to Amazon. In reality, the box started off at $209.70, the standard MSRP for a Universes Beyond box.

That brings the price-per-pack from $6.99, all the way down to $3.50 - a 50% price cut.

Next up, The Hobbit brought us back to Middle-Earth after our (excellent) first time visiting with The Lord of the Rings set, and you can save big on a Booster Box.

Again, Amazon says it’s a 12% discount but that doesn’t take into account the MSRP of $209.70. So you’re actually saving a bunch more than that when paying $142.08 .

In terms of per-pack, you’re paying $4.74 for each, but this set has the added advantage of a Box Topper card.

Finally for Play Booster Boxes, Reality Fracture is discounted . It’s an awesome set (one that maybe deserved more chance to shine…) and includes Mirrorverse versions of classic Magic: The Gathering spells, characters, and creatures.

It’s now $125.08, reduced from $139.65, meaning each pack costs you $4.17.

Also reduced in the Black Friday sale is the Magic: The Gathering Foundations Starter Collection .

This is a box of more than 350 cards, including a bunch of staples for building your own decks, and is an ideal purchase for anyone new to the game who wants an instant collection.

It’s usually $59.99, but with a 25% saving, it’s down to $44.95 - and I can wholeheartedly recommend it.

articles.title: The Sony PlayStation DualSense Edge Controller Drops to $152 Exclusively at Lenovo for Black Friday
articles.summary: Worth it for Grand Theft Auto 6.
articles.body:
Sony's official professional grade PlayStation DualSense Edge controller is much nicer than the standard DualSense controller, and a worthy upgrade for the upcoming Grand Theft Auto 6 game, but it retails for $200. The PlayStation Sale that went live earlier this weeked dropped the price to $169.99, but there's an even better deal today. Lenovo is currently offering it for just $152.09 with free shipping after you apply a 10% off coupon code " LENOVOBIGHOLIDAY ".

Black Friday Deal: 24% Off Sony PlayStation DualSense Edge

The DualSense Edge is Sony's official high-end controller for the PS5 console. It offers pro-level features like grips, adjustable analog sticks, mappable rear buttons, profiles, and more. They're very useful for gamers who invest time into esports or enjoy playing competitive games like first person shooters and fighting games .

One of the most important features of any pro controller are the thumbsticks and triggers. The sticks on the DualSense Edge are interchangeable; you can choose domed or convex replacements that come in two different heights. If your analog sticks crap out, you can buy replacements for $19.99 . The DualSense Edge comes standard with traditional potentiometer-based analog sticks, but some third party manufacturers now make aftermarket TMR versions .

There are also two sets of interchangeable back buttons that can be mapped to any button on the DualSense Edge controller. For Grand Theft Auto 6, the paddle switches might be used for weapon switching, sprinting or rolling in firefights, braking during car chases, or other actions that might normally force you to take your thumbs of the sticks.

The triggers, likewise, have received special treatment as well. Next to each trigger is a stop slider that lets you adjust how far you have to press the trigger down to make it register. You can choose standard, medium, or short travel distances.

Accessories include a hard shell case anda 9 foot long USB-C cable. All-in-all, it's a significant upgrade from the standard DualSense controller and, with this deal, worth the price premium.
